title: Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC)
subtitle: How long from putting money out to getting money back?
openingQuestion: What does a CCC of 45 days mean?
openingOptions: From buying materials to collecting cash takes 45 days - capital is tied up for 45 days
explanation: The cash conversion cycle measures the number of days your money is tied up: add the days inventory sits to the days spent waiting for customers to pay, then subtract the days you are allowed to owe your suppliers. The shorter the cycle, the less capital you need to run the same level of revenue. A negative cycle - Amazon, Costco - means the business collects before it has to pay, so the supply chain is funding it for free, and the faster it grows the more cash it accumulates.

diagram.label: DSO: days to collect from customers

realWorldExample.description: Amazon's CCC is negative: it collects on a sale almost at once (T+1-2) but pays suppliers after 45-90 days. So Amazon funds its growth with suppliers' money and needs no net working capital.

quiz.question: DSO is 60 days in an industry where 30 is normal. What does that mean?
options: Goods are being sold faster than at competitors
Collection is markedly slower than rivals, tying capital up longer
Inventory is turning over at half the usual rate
The business is paying its suppliers faster than it needs to
quiz.explanation: A DSO above the industry means collection is inefficient, or that a lot has to be sold on credit to stay competitive. The risks: rising bad debt and a shortage of cash. Compare against peers and against the trend over time.

quiz.question: Why does a company with a large positive Cash Conversion Cycle (say 90 days) need considerably more working capital than one with a CCC near zero, even when both have the same revenue?
options: Because the long-CCC company pays a higher rate on its bank debt
Because storage costs rise with the number of days
Because it must bridge all 90 days before the money returns
Because the long-CCC company recognises its revenue later
quiz.explanation: CCC essentially measures "how long capital stays tied up" in the operating cycle - the longer the CCC, the more working capital a company needs on hand to "bridge" the stretch between paying money out and collecting it back.

quiz.question: DIO 70, DSO 50, DPO 40 days. What is the CCC?
options: 20 days (forgetting DPO)
160 days (= 70 + 50 + 40, adding all three)
60 days (= 70 − 50 + 40, signs the wrong way)
quiz.explanation: CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO = 70 + 50 − 40 = 80 days. The company's money sits outside the till for 80 days per cycle - and every extra unit of revenue needs more capital to feed that same gap.

quiz.question: Which way of shortening the CCC does the least damage to relationships?
options: Selling faster, so inventory days come down
Delaying payments to suppliers
Tightening credit limits on every existing customer
Discounting heavily so customers agree to pay immediately
quiz.explanation: The three levers are not equivalent: squeezing suppliers and tightening up on customers are both paid for in relationships, whereas selling faster improves all three figures at once without putting anyone out.

quiz.question: Why did Amazon once operate with a negative CCC?
options: Because they held no inventory in any warehouse at all
Because customers paid at once while suppliers waited weeks
Because they collected from suppliers before selling the goods
Because revenue grew faster than the cost of capital did
quiz.explanation: Goods sold within a few days and card payments cleared immediately, but suppliers were paid after 60 days. The more they sold, the more free money they had to use - growth funding itself instead of consuming capital.

keyTakeaways: A short CCC: capital turns fast, so less of it is needed
A negative CCC is ideal - customers pay first, suppliers are paid later

practicePrompt.question: A company has DSO = 35 days (collecting from customers), DIO = 45 days (holding inventory), DPO = 30 days (paying suppliers). What is this company's Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC), in days?
options: CCC = DSO + DIO − DPO = 35 + 45 − 30 = 50 days
CCC = DSO + DIO + DPO = 35 + 45 + 30 = 110 days, adding all three periods together
CCC = DPO − DSO − DIO = 30 − 35 − 45 = −50 days, since DPO is always subtracted from first
CCC cannot be worked out without knowing the company's annual revenue
practicePrompt.explanation: CCC = DSO + DIO − DPO = 35 + 45 − 30 = 50 days. The company takes an average of 50 days from paying for goods to collecting the cash from selling them - the shorter the CCC, the less working capital it needs to sustain the same revenue.

summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a sentence rather than as a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: A short CCC: capital turns fast, so less of it is needed

application.title: Work out the CCC for your own business
application.message: If you run a shop, an online store, or freelance work where money in and money out are out of step, try estimating it: how many days from paying for goods or materials to collecting the cash - that is your real CCC.
application.secondary: The shorter your CCC, the less pressure there is to borrow just to keep operating.

sections.text: The Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC) answers a very concrete question: from the moment a business pays for raw materials to the moment it collects cash from a customer, how long does that take? The figure determines how much working capital the business needs to run smoothly.
The CCC formula and what each part means

CCC = DSO (Days Sales Outstanding - days taken to collect from customers) + DIO (Days Inventory Outstanding - days inventory sits in the warehouse) − DPO (Days Payable Outstanding - days taken to pay suppliers). The shorter the CCC, the faster capital turns and the less working capital a business needs to sustain the same revenue. If a company's DSO is 60 days while the industry average is only 30, that is a sign it collects less efficiently, or that it has to sell heavily on credit to compete - bringing with it a higher risk of bad debt and of running short of cash.
A negative CCC: a rare financial advantage

A company with a large positive CCC (say 90 days) needs considerably more working capital than one whose CCC is near zero, even at the same revenue - because throughout those 90 days of waiting to be paid, it still needs capital to keep operating. Amazon is the textbook case of a negative CCC: it collects on sales almost immediately (T+1-2 days) but pays suppliers after 45-90 days - meaning Amazon uses its suppliers' own money to fund its growth, and needs no net working capital.

items: A short or negative CCC: a major financial advantage, with growth not dependent on borrowing
A long CCC: needs substantial working capital on hand to 'bridge' the stretch between paying out and collecting in
Comparing CCC against competitors in the same industry matters more than the absolute figure

lines: Amazon and Walmart are not rich merely because they sell a lot - they are rich because they worked out how to have someone else fund their working capital.
